name: The Mars Scout Program
short_status: Ended without a third competition: two missions were selected, Phoenix in 2003 and MAVEN in 2008, and NASA opened Discovery to Mars in 2010. Both have now finished, MAVEN declared unrecoverable on 3 June 2026.
tagline: NASA · United States · Programme · 2000 · The long occupation Ended
stats: missions ever selected: Phoenix in 2003 and MAVEN in 2008
total mission cost cap on the first Scout competition, raised to $475m for the second
third Scout competitions held. Mars was folded into Discovery in 2010

facts.label: What a competed programme line is
facts.value: A standing, pre-authorised pot of money that NASA advertises rather than assigns. NASA issues an Announcement of Opportunity with a firm total mission cost cap and a launch deadline; any team may propose; a principal investigator, usually a working scientist rather than a NASA centre, leads the proposal and owns the science; NASA funds a handful of concept studies and then picks one to fly. The opposite is a directed or strategic mission, where NASA decides what it wants, assigns it to a centre, and asks Congress for a new start. Discovery, created in 1992, was the first planetary line run this way. Dates below are dates of record; where a clock time appears it is marked as local or UTC.

facts.label: Creation
facts.value: Announced in NASA release 00-171 on 26 October 2000, as part of the Mars Exploration Program that Scott Hubbard rebuilt after the loss of Mars Climate Orbiter and Mars Polar Lander in 1999. The wording: "NASA also proposes to create a new line of small 'Scout' missions which would be selected from proposals from the science community, and might involve airborne vehicles or small landers, as an investigation platform... The first Scout mission launch is planned for 2007."

facts.label: The 2001 open call
facts.value: On 20 July 2001 NASA funded ten concepts out of 43 proposals, at up to $150,000 each against a $300 million cost cap, chosen by Ed Weiler. They were SCIM (Laurie Leshin, Arizona State), KittyHawk (Wendy Calvin, Nevada-Reno), Urey (Jeff Plescia, USGS), MACO (Robert Kursinski, Arizona), Artemis (David Paige, UCLA), MEO (M. Janssen, JPL), Pascal (Rob Haberle, NASA Ames), Mars Scout Radar (Bruce Campbell, Smithsonian), The Naiades (Bob Grimm, Blackhawk GeoServices) and CryoScout (Frank Carsey, JPL). Hubbard's description of the exercise: "The intent of these studies was to open wide the door for fresh new ideas. There was almost no constraint given on the type of missions which could be proposed or selected for study."

facts.label: The first Announcement of Opportunity
facts.value: 25 proposals arrived in August 2002. On 6 December 2002, NASA release 02-238 named four for six-month implementation feasibility studies at up to $500,000 each, against a total mission cost cap of $325 million and a launch deadline of 31 December 2007. NASA described the exercise in a phrase worth keeping: "NASA's Mars 2007 Scout selection process is the first fully competed opportunity for scientific missions to the Red Planet."

facts.label: Phoenix wins
facts.value: 4 August 2003, NASA release 03-256. Ed Weiler selected Phoenix, a stationary polar lander led by Peter Smith of the University of Arizona, in partnership with JPL, Lockheed Martin and the Canadian Space Agency, built around the airframe of the cancelled Mars Surveyor 2001 lander. NASA called it "NASA's first fully competed opportunity for a dedicated science-driven mission". It launched on 4 August 2007 and landed on 25 May 2008.

facts.label: SCIM, the sample return with no lander
facts.value: Sample Collection for Investigation of Mars, led by Laurie Leshin of Arizona State University. It would have flown through the Martian upper atmosphere without landing or entering orbit, catching dust and gas in aerogel as Stardust and Genesis had done, and used a free-return trajectory to bring the capsule back to Earth. NASA's own description said such samples "could provide breakthrough understanding of the chemistry of Mars, its surface, atmosphere, interior evolution and potential biological activity". SCIM got no further than that six-month, $500,000 concept study; no SCIM hardware was built.

facts.label: ARES, the aeroplane
facts.value: Aerial Regional-scale Environmental Survey, led by Joel Levine at NASA Langley Research Center. A rocket-powered aircraft that would have been delivered in a Pathfinder-derived aeroshell by a Genesis-derived flyby spacecraft, unfolded in the atmosphere, and flown about 1.5 km above the ground at 140 m/s for up to 101 minutes and 850 km. The reference design gives the airframe at 6.2 m wingspan, 66.5 kg dry and 125 kg wet, on a Delta 2925 with a 678 kg wet launch mass. The proposed payload was a magnetometer resolving crustal magnetism at 2 km and 1 nT, a mass spectrometer good to 1 part per billion, a neutron spectrometer, an ionizing radiation detector, an atmospheric data system, and context and video cameras.

facts.label: ARES actually flew, on Earth
facts.value: A half-scale prototype called the ARES Eagle was carried by balloon from Naval Air Station Tillamook, Oregon at 10:15 local time on 19 September 2002, released at about 11:49 from close to 19 miles up with its wings and tail folded as they would have been inside the aeroshell, unfolded, transitioned from free fall to horizontal flight, flew a pre-programmed course and landed undamaged at 13:28. This is further than most losing proposals ever get.

facts.label: MARVEL, the methane hunter
facts.value: Mars Volcanic Emission and Life Scout, led by Mark Allen of JPL. An orbiter carrying two instrument types already proven looking at Earth's atmosphere from orbit: a solar occultation infrared spectrometer with very high sensitivity to methane, and a submillimetre spectrometer that could survey continuously through dust storms and polar night and was very sensitive to water vapour, to find localised places where subsurface water might be venting. That is close to the job Europe's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter was eventually built to do. MARVEL itself got no further than the six-month concept study.

facts.label: The second Announcement of Opportunity
facts.value: Proposals were due in August 2006 and on 8 January 2007 NASA funded two nine-month concept studies at about $2 million each, against a cap of no more than $475 million for a 2011 launch: MAVEN, principal investigator Bruce Jakosky of the University of Colorado at Boulder with project management at Goddard, and The Great Escape, principal investigator Alan Stern of the Southwest Research Institute. The same announcement funded an instrument contribution to Europe's ExoMars and two technology studies. NASA's 2007 release says 26 proposals were received in August 2006; NASA's 2008 MAVEN release says the winner was chosen from 20 mission investigation proposals submitted to the same call. The 2007 selection also covered non-mission proposals, which probably reconciles the two counts, but we found no source that says so.

facts.label: The Great Escape
facts.value: TGE would have measured the escape of the Martian upper atmosphere. NASA's own wording is that both finalists "would provide similar measurements of Mars' upper atmosphere, including its dynamics and evolution, which have been given a high priority by the scientific community". NASA's January 2007 release names Alan Stern of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder as principal investigator, with project management at SwRI in San Antonio. Stern moved to NASA Headquarters as associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate in April 2007 and left the proposal; by NASA's December 2007 release the principal investigator was Jim Burch of SwRI in San Antonio. Neither release states the date or the terms on which he stepped down.

facts.label: The conflict of interest
facts.value: In November 2007, shortly after the two concept study reports were received, NASA postponed the evaluation to resolve what it described only as an organizational conflict of interest in one team's Phase A concept study. It judged the conflict severe enough that its only recourse was to stop the evaluation and reconstitute the entire review panel that provides technical and cost analyses for mission selections. On 21 December 2007, in release 07-283, NASA announced that the roughly four-month delay had made a 2011 launch unachievable and moved the mission to 2013. Michael Meyer: "The panel's independent expertise and evaluation are critical to maintaining a fair and competitive mission selection process." NASA has never published which team was involved.

facts.label: MAVEN wins
facts.value: Revised proposals were due in August 2008 and NASA announced the selection on 15 September 2008: the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN spacecraft, $485 million, for a late 2013 launch, chosen as "the best science value and lowest implementation risk". The University of Colorado received $6 million for a year of mission planning, Goddard managed the project, and Lockheed Martin built the spacecraft on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and 2001 Mars Odyssey designs. The $485 million figure is $10 million above the $475 million cap stated in the 2007 call, and we found no source explaining the difference.

facts.label: Why there was no third competition
facts.value: Two decisions taken elsewhere closed the line. NASA and ESA agreed in 2009 to run their Mars programmes together as the Mars Exploration Joint Initiative, committing the Mars launch opportunities from 2016 onward to joint missions, so the slot a third Scout would have used was already spoken for. SpaceNews, reporting the first product of that agreement in August 2010, wrote that the cooperative strategy "comes at the price of NASA's Mars Scout series of missions, which will be discontinued after the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution (MAVEN) mission". And NASA's Science Mission Directorate opened Discovery to Mars: the final Discovery Announcement of Opportunity NNH10ZDA007O, released on 7 June 2010 after a draft, NNH10ZDA003J, in December 2009, states that "The proposed missions may target any body in the Solar System, including Mars and Earth's Moon, but excluding the Earth and Sun." The 2010 announcement even sets rules for missions to the Martian surface.

facts.label: How the end was recorded
facts.value: The 2011 planetary science decadal survey, Vision and Voyages for Planetary Science in the Decade 2013-2022, states it twice: "NASA does not intend to continue the Mars Scout program beyond the MAVEN mission, and instead plans to include Mars in the Discovery Program", and "We note that NASA does not intend to continue the Mars Scout program beyond the MAVEN mission, nor do we recommend that they do so. Instead, the committee recommends that NASA continue to allow Discovery missions to be proposed to all planetary bodies, including Mars." Elsewhere the same report says of Scout that "Subsequently, the program was combined with Discovery."

facts.label: What it became
facts.value: On 20 August 2012, in release 12-288, NASA selected InSight as the twelfth Discovery mission from 28 proposals submitted to the June 2010 call, capped at $425 million in 2010 dollars excluding launch. NASA's own wording is that "InSight builds on spacecraft technology used in NASA's highly successful Phoenix lander mission". The Scout line's last descendant is therefore a mission selected under a different programme using the first Scout mission's spacecraft design.

facts.label: Both Scout missions are over
facts.value: NASA's Phoenix mission page gives the end of mission as 2 November 2008, the date of the lander's last signal. JPL's release of 24 May 2010 closed the file: a final listening campaign of 61 Mars Odyssey overflights detected nothing, and orbital images showed the lander smaller and its solar arrays apparently damaged by winter carbon-dioxide ice. MAVEN fell silent in December 2025; NASA's anomaly review board concluded the spacecraft could not be recovered, and NASA announced the end of the mission on 3 June 2026, stating that "the MAVEN spacecraft is not recoverable, and it is no longer capable of performing its science and data relay mission". The Scout line has no working hardware left at Mars. Checked 24 August 2026.

timeline: NASA release 00-171 announces the rebuilt Mars Exploration Program, including "a new line of small 'Scout' missions which would be selected from proposals from the science community", with the first launch planned for 2007.

Ten concepts funded for study out of 43 proposals, at up to $150,000 each against a $300 million cost cap: SCIM, KittyHawk, Urey, MACO, Artemis, MEO, Pascal, Mars Scout Radar, The Naiades and CryoScout.

A half-scale ARES prototype is dropped from a balloon at nearly 19 miles over Tillamook, Oregon, unfolds its wings and tail, flies a pre-programmed course and lands undamaged. The proposal it belongs to will lose.

Four of 25 proposals go to six-month studies against a $325 million cap: SCIM, ARES, Phoenix and MARVEL. NASA calls it "the first fully competed opportunity for scientific missions to the Red Planet".

Phoenix is selected as the first Mars Scout mission, a polar lander led by Peter Smith of the University of Arizona built on the cancelled Mars Surveyor 2001 airframe. It will launch exactly four years later and land on 25 May 2008.

Two finalists funded at about $2 million each for nine-month concept studies against a $475 million cap and a 2011 launch: MAVEN under Bruce Jakosky and The Great Escape under Alan Stern. Both would measure atmospheric escape.

Alan Stern, principal investigator of The Great Escape, becomes NASA associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate and leaves the proposal. By NASA's December 2007 release Jim Burch of SwRI in San Antonio is its principal investigator.

Shortly after the concept study reports arrive, NASA finds an organizational conflict of interest in one of the two teams' studies, stops the evaluation and reconstitutes the entire technical and cost review panel.
NASA announces that the four-month delay has made a 2011 launch unachievable and moves the second Scout mission to 2013. Revised proposals are set for August 2008 and selection for December 2008.
MAVEN is selected at $485 million for a late 2013 launch. It is the last Mars Scout selection ever made.

The Discovery 2010 Announcement of Opportunity is released, stating that proposals "may target any body in the Solar System, including Mars and Earth's Moon". No third Scout announcement is ever issued.

InSight is selected as the twelfth Discovery mission, capped at $425 million in 2010 dollars, and NASA notes that it "builds on spacecraft technology used in NASA's highly successful Phoenix lander mission". The competed low-cost Mars mission survives, under another programme's name.

images.caption: A HiRISE image from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing Phoenix hanging beneath its parachute during descent on 25 May 2008, with a 10 km crater informally named Heimdall filling the frame behind it and a full-resolution inset of the parachute and lander at lower left. JPL's caption notes that although Phoenix appears to be descending into the crater it is actually about 20 km in front of it.

A colour photograph of 23 August 2013 showing the MAVEN spacecraft standing on its rotation fixture inside the Payload Hazardous Servicing Facility at Kennedy Space Center ahead of testing and launch preparations, its instrument booms and blanketed bus exposed and its solar arrays not yet fitted. Mission plaques for NASA, Mars Global Surveyor, Stardust and Mars Science Laboratory hang on the wall behind it.
images.credit: NASA/Chris Rhodes, as given in NASA's own caption (KSC-2013-3455)

images.caption: A colour photograph of the ARES Mars Eagle, the half-scale drop-test aeroplane, sitting on a wooden cradle on wet tarmac in fog with its wings spread and red-tipped, a vertical tail below the fuselage and a silver DC-3 parked behind it. NASA Langley's own caption for the frame reads: ARES Mars Eagle on the morning of the high altitude drop test with DC-3 in background.
images.credit: NASA Langley Research Center, ARES project website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine

images.caption: An onboard video frame looking forward along the wing of the ARES Mars Eagle in flight, with the curve of the Earth's limb and the dark sky of the upper atmosphere across the top of the picture and cloud and terrain far below. NASA Langley's own caption for the frame reads: ARES Mars Eagle descending over Oregon during its high altitude flight test.
images.credit: NASA Langley Research Center, ARES project website, via the Internet Archive Wayback Machine

images.caption: An artist's rendering released by JPL as PIA07085 under the title Concept for Mars Volcanic Emission Life Scout, showing a three-panel orbiter above a dark Martian landscape with instrument sight lines reaching down to a glowing vent and a circular inset detail of a fissure in the ground. NASA's own summary describes it as an artist's rendition of a concept for a Mars orbiter that would scrutinise the atmosphere for chemical traces of life or of environments that could support life.
